cases.excerpt: To examine the relation of the total intake of fluids and the types of beverages to the risk of bladder cancer, we conducted a hospital based case-control study with 130 newly diagnosed bladder cancer patients and the same number of matched controls.

comparison.excerpt: Information of total fluid intake was derived from the reported frequency of consumption of the different types of beverages on the food frequency questionnaire.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Multivariate logistic regression model showed consumption of: soda (OR=8.32; 95%CI=3.18-21.76), coffee (OR=1.46; 95%CI=1.05-2.01) and spirits (OR=1.15; 95%CI=1.04-1.28) as statistically significant risk factors, while mineral water (OR=0.52; 95%CI=0.34-0.79), skim milk (OR=0.38; 95%CI=0.16-0.91), yogurt (OR=0.34; 95%CI=0.12-0.97) and frequency of daily urination (OR=0.27; 95%CI=0.18-0.41) were statistically significant protective variables.

cases.excerpt: Thirteen cohort studies, included in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study, provided data for 3590 BC cases and 593,637 non-cases.

comparison.excerpt: comparing those in the moderate (25-85 g/day) and high categories (>85 g/day) with non-consumers

confidence_interval.excerpt: However, an inverse association was observed between yoghurt consumption and BC risk when comparing those in the moderate (25-85 g/day) and high categories (>85 g/day) with non-consumers, with multivariate HR of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.75-0.96) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.78-0.98), respectively.

design.excerpt: a pooled analysis of 13 cohort studies

effect_size.excerpt: However, an inverse association was observed between yoghurt consumption and BC risk when comparing those in the moderate (25-85 g/day) and high categories (>85 g/day) with non-consumers, with multivariate HR of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.75-0.96) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.78-0.98), respectively. We found no evidence of association between either total or individual dairy products and BC risk, but suggestive evidence that consumption of yoghurt may be associated with a decreased risk.

studies.Study: Larsson SC et al. (2008) [PMID: 18842797] — estimate 2 · Female
studies.Title: Cultured milk, yogurt, and dairy intake in relation to bladder cancer risk in a prospective study of Swedish women and men.

combined_p_value_resolution.method: Two-sided Wald test on the log ratio (null 1), using the 95% CI width.
Two-sided Wald test on the log ratio (null 1), using the 95% CI width.

combined_source_extraction.comparison_type: ≥2 servings/d vs 0 serving/d of cultured milk
combined_source_extraction.ethnicity_basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available

cases.excerpt: During a mean follow-up of 9.4 y, 485 participants (76 women and 409 men) were diagnosed with bladder cancer.

comparison.excerpt: highest category of cultured milk intake (> or =2 servings/d) compared with the lowest category (0 serving/d)

confidence_interval.excerpt: The multivariate RRs for the highest category of cultured milk intake (> or =2 servings/d) compared with the lowest category (0 serving/d) were 0.62 (95% CI: 0.46, 0.85; P for trend = 0.006) in women and men combined, 0.55 (95% CI: 0.25, 1.22; P for trend = 0.06) in women, and 0.64 (95% CI: 0.46, 0.89; P for trend = 0.03) in men.

effect_size.excerpt: The multivariate RRs for the highest category of cultured milk intake (> or =2 servings/d) compared with the lowest category (0 serving/d) were 0.62 (95% CI: 0.46, 0.85; P for trend = 0.006) in women and men combined, 0.55 (95% CI: 0.25, 1.22; P for trend = 0.06) in women, and 0.64 (95% CI: 0.46, 0.89; P for trend = 0.03) in men. The intake of milk or cheese was not associated with bladder cancer risk.

timing.excerpt: We prospectively followed 82,002 Swedish women and men
